Trying to Conceive

When Are the Best Times to Conceive? Fertile Window

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When are the best times to conceive? Your fertile window covers the five days before ovulation and ovulation day itself. The highest chance is usually in the one to two days before the egg is released. Sperm can live for up to five days inside the body, while the egg lasts only about 12 to 24 hours. This guide turns that biology into a simple schedule you can follow, whatever your cycle length.

Why the window is six days

The fertile window exists because sperm and egg have very different lifespans. Sperm can survive up to five days inside the uterus and fallopian tubes, especially around ovulation when conditions favor them. The egg is far less patient: once released, it lasts roughly 12 to 24 hours. Put those two facts together and you get about six days each cycle when sex can lead to pregnancy, the five days before ovulation plus ovulation day itself. Sex after that day rarely results in pregnancy, because by the time new sperm arrive, the egg is usually gone.

Within those six days, the odds are not spread evenly. The strongest days are the one to two days just before ovulation, when sperm are already in place as the egg is released. This is why timing that feels too early usually is not. Sperm that arrive ahead of the egg can wait for it. Sperm that arrive a day late usually cannot catch it. If you take one idea from this page, take this one: the goal is to have sperm waiting before ovulation happens, not to race the egg afterward. Everything else in your schedule follows from that.

Find your likely ovulation day

Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before your next period starts, not 14 days after your last one began. The difference matters, because the first half of the cycle varies a lot between people while the second half is fairly steady. To estimate your ovulation day, take your usual cycle length and subtract 14, counting from day one, the first day of full bleeding. A 28 day cycle points to ovulation around day 14. A 26 day cycle points to around day 12. A 32 day cycle points to around day 18, which surprises many people who assume day 14 applies to everyone.

Once you have an estimated ovulation day, count back five days to find the start of your window. For a 26 day cycle, that is roughly days 7 to 12. For a 28 day cycle, days 9 to 14. For a 32 day cycle, days 13 to 18. Treat these as estimates, not appointments, because ovulation can shift a few days even in regular cycles. If your cycle length varies, use your shortest and longest recent cycles to bracket the window. The ovulation calculator in BeMama can do this math for you and adjust the dates as you log each new period.

A schedule that does not take over your life

The advice most clinicians give is refreshingly simple: have sex every one to two days during the fertile window. That rhythm keeps healthy sperm present across the whole window without demanding a daily performance. Daily sex is fine if you both want it, but it is not required, and forcing it tends to drain the fun out of a month fast. Long gaps matter more than perfect spacing. If life only allows a couple of tries this cycle, put them in the two to three days ending on your estimated ovulation day, since those dates carry the best chance.

Starting early beats starting late. Because sperm can wait for the egg but the egg cannot wait for sperm, begin a day or two before you think the window opens rather than holding out for one perfect day. Some couples skip tracking altogether and simply have sex every two to three days through the whole cycle. That approach covers the window automatically and removes the deadline feeling, which some people find easier to live with. There is no single right method here. Pick the version that suits your relationship and your energy, and remember that showing up across several cycles matters more than precision in any single one.

What helps, and what is folklore

No position has been shown to improve the chance of pregnancy. Sperm reach the cervix within minutes regardless of how you have sex, and there is no reliable evidence that lying down afterward, propping your hips on a pillow, or delaying a trip to the bathroom changes the outcome. If resting for a few minutes feels nice, do it because it feels nice. Orgasm is not required for conception either. These bits of folklore mostly add chores and worry to something that already carries enough of both, so feel free to let them go without guilt.

One small change may be worth making: lubricant. Some everyday lubricants can slow sperm in laboratory testing, so if you use one regularly, look for a product labeled fertility friendly, which is formulated to avoid that effect. Beyond the bedroom, a few basics help: neither partner smoking, skipping alcohol entirely if you are the one trying to become pregnant, since early pregnancy can go unnoticed for weeks, regular sleep where you can get it, and a daily 400 microgram folic acid supplement for the partner who will carry the pregnancy, since it lowers the risk of serious birth defects of the brain and spine that form in the earliest weeks. None of these are magic levers, and none need to be perfect. They simply stack the ordinary odds a little more in your favor while you work the calendar.

When to fine tune, and when to call a clinician

Calendar math works best when cycles are fairly regular. If yours vary by more than a few days, or you want to pinpoint the day instead of estimating it, ovulation predictor kits detect the hormone surge that happens shortly before the egg is released, and they are the natural next step once you know your rough window. Many people also learn to read their body's own signals across the cycle, which is a useful skill in its own right and one we cover separately. Neither tool is required to conceive. They simply replace guessing with measuring when guessing starts to feel thin.

Good timing cannot fix everything, and that is worth knowing early. If you are under 35 and have been trying for about a year without a pregnancy, book an appointment with your doctor or midwife. If you are 35 or older, go after about six months, and at 40 or older it is reasonable to talk with a clinician as soon as you decide to start trying. Go sooner at any age if your periods are irregular, absent, or very painful, if you have a known condition such as PCOS, endometriosis, or thyroid disease, or if either partner has a history that raises questions. An early conversation is information gathering, not a verdict, and it often starts with simple checks for both of you.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cycle length and ovulation timing vary, so calendar dates and home fertility signs provide estimates rather than proof. Temperature usually rises after ovulation, cervical mucus may change beforehand, and urine tests detect a hormone surge that suggests ovulation may follow.

Sleep disruption, illness, travel, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception, and irregular cycles can make patterns harder to interpret. Combining observations may provide useful context, but no home method confirms fertility or guarantees pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can place periods, temperatures, cervical mucus, symptoms, and test results on one timeline. Fertile-window dates are educational estimates and must not be used as contraception.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for persistently absent, very painful, unusually heavy, or highly irregular periods, or when a medical condition may affect fertility.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Evaluating Infertility

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • The fertile window is about six days: the five days before ovulation plus ovulation day itself.
  • Ovulation usually falls about 14 days before your next period, so subtract 14 from your cycle length.
  • Have sex every one to two days across the window, and start early rather than late.
  • Positions and lying down afterward do not change the odds, but a fertility friendly lubricant may be worth choosing.
  • See a clinician after a year of trying under 35, after six months at 35 to 39, right away at 40 or older, and sooner if cycles are irregular.

Frequently asked questions

How many days before ovulation can you get pregnant?

You can get pregnant from sex up to five days before ovulation, because sperm can survive that long inside the body. The highest chances come from the one to two days just before the egg is released. Earlier sex in the window still counts, since sperm can wait in the fallopian tubes until the egg arrives.

How often should you have sex when trying to conceive?

Every one to two days during the fertile window is the pace most clinicians recommend. Daily sex is fine if you both want it, but it is not required. If tracking feels stressful, sex every two to three days across the whole cycle covers the window automatically.

Can you get pregnant the day after ovulation?

It is possible but unlikely, because the egg survives only about 12 to 24 hours after release. By the day after ovulation, the window has usually closed for that cycle. This is why starting before ovulation matters far more than continuing after it.

What is the fertile window for a 32 day cycle?

In a 32 day cycle, ovulation usually lands around day 18, so the fertile window is roughly days 13 to 18. Estimate it by subtracting 14 from your cycle length, then counting back five days. If your cycles vary, an ovulation test can confirm the day itself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
